questions.q: In Scenario 1 (AD FS without OIDC support), why is SAML the correct protocol choice despite OIDC often being the more modern default?
options: OIDC cannot be used with Salesforce under any circumstances
AD FS cannot be used for SSO at all
SAML is always correct regardless of any infrastructure details
The existing AD FS deployment doesn't support OIDC, so the newer protocol simply isn't an option here, even though it's often preferred in general
questions.explain: A general preference for the modern protocol doesn't override a specific scenario constraint — if the existing identity infrastructure only speaks SAML, SAML is the only viable choice, regardless of what's generally preferred.

questions.q: In Scenario 2 (SSO into an expense tool from within Salesforce), which role must Salesforce play?
options: Identity Provider (IdP), since the expense tool is relying on Salesforce's authentication decision
Neither; this scenario doesn't involve SSO
Both roles simultaneously for the same login event
Service Provider (SP), since Salesforce is almost always the SP
questions.explain: Because the expense tool trusts a login that happened in Salesforce, Salesforce must be the IdP in this relationship — defaulting to 'Salesforce is always the SP' is the trap this scenario is designed to catch.

questions.q: In Scenario 3, what specifically made the admin's 'it worked for me' test insufficient before disabling standard login for everyone?
options: SAML SSO cannot be tested at all before full rollout
Testing with one's own account is always fully sufficient for any rollout
Testing with their own account before disabling login for all profiles leaves no verification that a break-glass path would survive an IdP outage for anyone, including that admin
The admin should have tested with a non-admin account only
questions.explain: A single successful test doesn't verify recovery behavior during an outage — disabling standard login broadly immediately afterward removes any break-glass path if the IdP later fails.

questions.q: In Scenario 4, why is JIT provisioning insufficient as a complete user lifecycle management solution?
options: JIT provisioning is identical to SCIM in every respect
JIT provisioning requires disabling SSO entirely
JIT provisioning cannot create any users at all
JIT only handles creation/update at login time; it does nothing for deactivation or for pre-provisioning access before a user's first login
questions.explain: JIT covers only a slice of the user lifecycle (creation/update at login), leaving deactivation and pre-provisioning needs uncovered — treating it as sufficient for the full lifecycle is the trap.

questions.q: What is the general pattern underlying all four wrong-answer traps described in this lesson?
options: Each trap over-generalizes a rule that's often true into a universal rule, without checking whether the specific scenario's details make it inapplicable
Each trap is caused by misconfiguring OAuth scopes
Each trap only applies to Experience Cloud scenarios
Each trap involves a factual error about Salesforce's technical capabilities
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly identifies the pattern as over-generalization: taking a frequently-true rule ('prefer modern protocols', 'Salesforce is often the SP', 'JIT automates provisioning') and applying it without checking the scenario's specific constraints.
